column11: derived: Merck generated $39,599mm of free cash flow on $189,294mm of revenue over 2023, 2024 and 2025, a 20.92% margin, against the 29.5% its cost of sales, SG&A and R&D leave. Solved so the modelled book reproduces that margin rather than assumed from one line's cost structure: the alliance rows carry no cost of sales and Animal Health carries its own, so a ratio taken off a single product does not reconcile the company. Restated before interest: MRK paid $3,700mm of interest inside operating cash flow over 2023 to 2025, 1.95% of revenue. The free cash flow above is struck after it and the valuation already charges the debt by subtracting net debt, so the charge falls by that much, from 12.10% to 10.14%. Restated at replacement capex: MRK spent $11,347mm on plant over 2023 to 2025 against $6,977mm of plant depreciation, 2.31% of revenue above what keeps the plant running. Taken at depreciation, the charge falls from 10.14% to 7.48%. Restated without one-off cash: MRK's free cash flow over 2023 to 2025 carried $8,300mm of deal payments in operating cash flow, capital allocation whose assets the book values separately; $572mm of legal settlements; $1,200mm of US transition tax (2025 instalment 1,200mm). None recurs, so the charge falls from 7.48% to 2.06%. Restated without working capital build: over 2023 to 2025 MRK's cash flow statement shows receivables up $2,482mm, inventories up $2,831mm, payables down $88mm, a working capital build of $5,401mm, 2.85% of revenue. Growth ties that cash up once, not on every product for ever, so the charge falls from 2.06% to -1.23%. Rebuilt on the book's own ratios on 0.3610 of the revenue they are struck on, against 0.3746 the filings leave as cash over 2023 to 2025 (free cash flow before interest, at replacement capex, without one-off cash and without working capital build), so the charge is -1.3576%.

column11: McDermott KW, Liang L, 'Overview of Major Ambulatory Surgeries Performed in Hospital-Owned Facilities, 2019', HCUP Statistical Brief #287, December 2021, Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, Rockville MD (hcup-us.ahrq.gov/reports/statbriefs/sb287-Ambulatory-Surgery-Overview-2019.jsp, read 2026-11-10): 'In 2019, 11.9 million encounters for major ambulatory surgeries took place in hospital-owned facilities.' Prevalence is stated equal to incidence because acute postoperative pain is the year's own procedures: a patient not treated in the year of the operation is not carried into the next
column12: A FLOOR, AND KNOWABLY SO. It counts hospital-owned facilities only, so it leaves out freestanding ambulatory surgery centres, and it leaves out inpatient surgery entirely. The companion brief on inpatient operating-room procedures (Weiss AJ, Jiang HJ, HCUP Statistical Brief #297, September 2022) reports rates per 100,000 rather than a national count, so no inpatient total could be added without computing one, and I did not. Postoperative Pain has no row in data/epidemiology.csv and no other seed in the book carries a pool for it

column11: the same HCUP Statistical Brief #287 figure, the same row as the prevalence above, on the convention stated there

two shares from one survey, multiplied. Gan TJ, Habib AS, Miller TE, White W, Apfelbaum JL, 'Incidence, patient satisfaction, and perceptions of post-surgical pain: results from a US national survey', Curr Med Res Opin 2014;30(1):149-160 (doi 10.1185/03007995.2013.860019, PMID 24237004), a random sample of 300 US adults who had surgery within five years: 'Of the 300 participants, ~86% experienced pain after surgery; of these, 75% had moderate/extreme pain during the immediate post-surgical period'. 0.86 x 0.75 = 0.645, about 7.68mm patients a year. NCT07862595 requires participants who report 'moderate or severe pain on the Pain Severity (Verbal Rating Scale)' and a score of 4 or more on the numeric rating scale, which is the same cut
column12: a weak survey and it should be read as one: 300 respondents, self-reported, with an average 14-month recall gap the authors name as a limitation, and the paper is twelve years old. It is the only free US figure for the moderate-to-severe share that I could open. The trial's own entry rules narrow much further than this (a primary unilateral bunionectomy with distal first metatarsal osteotomy, BMI 18 to under 40, regional anaesthesia, no prior foot surgery), but those are a pain model, not a label population, so they are deliberately not cut

column10: share of each year's eligible patients
column11: the measured share of the same population in which the incumbent analgesic is already failing, from the same survey: Gan TJ et al., Curr Med Res Opin 2014;30(1):149-160, 'Approximately 88% received analgesic medications to manage pain; of these, 80% experienced adverse effects and 39% reported moderate/severe pain even after receiving their first dose.' 0.39 is the share still in moderate or severe pain after the first dose of what they were given, which is the segment a new mechanism competes for first. NCT07862595 randomises MK-6916 against hydrocodone 5 mg with acetaminophen 325 mg, the incumbent that share describes
column12: A JUDGEMENT AND THE WEAKEST NUMBER IN THE FILE, AND IT ERRS HIGH. It hands MK-6916 the whole segment in which first-line analgesia fails, at peak, where in practice perioperative analgesia is formulary-controlled, bundled into the procedure payment, and would be contested by suzetrigine and by generic multimodal regimens. It errs low in one direction only: it leaves out the 80% who had adverse effects on their current analgesic, who are also switchable. A reader who wants a defensible lower bound should take a fraction of this rather than the whole of it

column12: case for higher: a bunionectomy study with SPID48 against both placebo and an active opioid comparator is the best-characterised analgesic model there is, and the endpoint is read at 48 hours rather than over months. Case for lower: the trial has not started (NOT_YET_RECRUITING, estimated start 2026-11-23), Merck has published nothing on the mechanism, and the exclusions for Brugada syndrome, unexplained syncope, structural heart disease and cardiac dysrhythmia point at a cardiac liability the base rate does not know about

column11: NCT07862595 (ClinicalTrials.gov API v2, read 2026-11-10) doses MK-6916 as a '120 mg or 70 mg oral tablet given every 12 hours (q12h) for 48 hours' for acute pain after bunionectomy, with the sum of pain intensity difference over 0 to 48 hours as the primary outcome. Acute postoperative pain is bought as a course. Journavx, the one approved non-opioid in the class, is labelled 'not studied beyond 14 days', and vrtx_journavx_price.csv states the basis: annualising it would invent a quantity nobody buys
column12: one_time, so the engine reads the year's new patients as the year's revenue. A patient who has two operations in a year buys two courses and is counted once, which understates volume rather than flattering it

column11: a measured chain on the only non-opioid approved for moderate to severe acute pain, in the same pain model. Suzetrigine's Phase 2 bunionectomy study NCT04977336 reached actual primary completion 2022-02-17, and Journavx was approved 2025-01-30 (NDA 219209, openFDA, the date the book's approvals table holds), 1,078 days later. MK-6916's own Phase 2 bunionectomy study NCT07862595 has estimated primary completion 2027-06-10; 1,078 days on is 2030-05-23, so 2031 is the first full year on sale
column12: one drug's history, not a distribution, and suzetrigine's was fast: its Phase 3 bunionectomy study NCT05553366 completed 2023-12-15 and the NDA was acted on 13.5 months after that. MK-6916 has no Phase 3 on file at all, so the chain assumes one starts promptly on a positive Phase 2 and runs as quickly. It is not yet recruiting, estimated start 2026-11-23

column11: comparator: Journavx (suzetrigine), the only non-opioid approved for moderate to severe acute pain and the class MK-6916 would enter. Its wholesale acquisition cost is $15.50 per 50 mg pill and a typical seven-day course is $232.50, which is fifteen pills and reconciles to the label's 100 mg loading dose followed by 50 mg every 12 hours (ICER's review of suzetrigine, PMC12204333; the figure data/assumptions/vrtx_journavx_price.csv carries, sourced in vrtx_journavx.csv to Vertex's own release on approval, 2025-01-30). $232.50 is 0.0002325mm
column12: the course length is Journavx's, not MK-6916's: no label exists and NCT07862595 doses only 48 hours, which is the pain model rather than a course. Journavx's labelled outer limit, fourteen days, is twenty-nine pills at $449.50 and would nearly double this. A seven-day MK-6916 course at twelve-hourly dosing is fourteen tablets against Journavx's fifteen, so the two are comparable pill for pill; the per-tablet price of a different molecule is not, and no price for MK-6916 exists

column11: Part D gross-to-net convention, measured at a median 96% of CMS's own negotiated net annual prices across the nine cycle-one IRA drugs (backend/gross_to_net.py, PART_D_CONVENTION). CMS spending is gross of the rebates a manufacturer pays, and half is what the book takes off it, the rate vrtx_journavx.csv carries for suzetrigine. Cross-checked on Vertex's own figures: $59.6mm of FY2025 Journavx product revenue over 'more than 550,000 prescriptions' written and filled since pharmacy availability in March 2025 (10-K 0000875320-26-000056) is $108.36 a prescription, 46.6% of the $232.50 wholesale acquisition cost of a seven-day course
column12: the wholesale acquisition cost above is gross, so half comes off and the net course is $116.25. The cross-check takes one prescription as one seven-day course and ignores channel inventory, so it supports the size of the deduction rather than measuring it. A branded entrant in a class of generic opioids and non-steroidal anti-inflammatories buys formulary access with rebates, which is the case for a deeper cut
